section.title: Deliver Me, O Lord
section.sectionRationale: The first psalm to carry a historical superscription (during Absalom's rebellion), and the model lament of the Psalter: a cry of distress that moves through confidence to sleep in peace and a closing benediction over God's people.
section.thesis: Surrounded by many enemies, David finds that the LORD is a shield around him, so that he can lie down and sleep even under threat, and he prays for deliverance while confessing that salvation belongs to the LORD alone.
section.frameNote: Four short movements marked by Selah: the crisis of many foes (vv1-2), confidence in the LORD as shield and sustainer (vv3-6), a prayer for deliverance (v7), and the closing confession that salvation and blessing belong to the LORD (v8).

units.label: Many foes have risen
units.note: God will not deliver him, they say

verses.text: O LORD, how my foes have increased! How many rise up against me!
Many say of me, "God will not deliver him." {{selah|Selah}}

units.label: The LORD is my shield
units.note: I lie down and sleep, for the LORD sustains me

verses.text: But You, O LORD, are a shield around me, my glory, and the One who lifts my head.
To the LORD I cry aloud, and He answers me from His holy mountain. {{selah|Selah}}
I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me.
I will not fear the myriads set against me on every side.
Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God! Strike all my enemies on the jaw; break the teeth of the wicked.
Salvation belongs to the LORD; may Your blessing be on Your people. {{selah|Selah}}

selah.gloss: A musical or liturgical marker of uncertain exact meaning, likely calling for a pause, a lifting of voices, or an instrumental interlude. Here it punctuates the psalm's turn from complaint to confidence and from confidence to closing praise, inviting the singer to pause and let each truth settle.

basic.context: Psalm 3 carries the Psalter's first historical superscription: a psalm of David when he fled from his son Absalom. Surrounded by enemies who say God will not save him, David declares the LORD his shield, sleeps in peace under threat, and prays for deliverance, closing with the confession that salvation belongs to the LORD alone.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a lament, a genuine cry of distress addressed to God, not a private complaint hidden from Him; the Psalms teach that pouring out real fear and asking for God to strike enemies is honest, Spirit-shaped prayer, not sub-Christian venting, though the New Testament reframes personal vengeance as belonging to God alone, Romans 12:19.
basic.originalLanguages: Three times the psalm is marked by selah, a pause inviting reflection, at the turn from complaint to confidence, from confidence to prayer, and at the closing confession. The image of God as a shield around David and the one who lifts his head pictures both protection and restored dignity.
basic.typology: David, betrayed by his own son and hunted by those closest to him, foreshadows Christ, betrayed by Judas and abandoned by His own, who also entrusted Himself to the Father and could sleep, even the sleep of death, in perfect confidence of vindication.
basic.christ: Jesus prayed psalms like this one from the cross, facing enemies who mocked, 'He trusts in God, let God deliver Him' echoes the taunt David faced; Christ's own resurrection is the ultimate answer to David's cry that salvation belongs to the LORD.
basic.god: God is pictured here as shield, glory, and the one who lifts the bowed head, an intensely personal defender who answers prayer from His holy mountain even while enemies multiply on every side.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Samuel 15-17 narrates Absalom's rebellion behind this psalm. Matthew 27:43 echoes the taunt that God will not deliver the sufferer. Romans 12:19 reframes vengeance as belonging to God rather than to us.
basic.oneStory: Psalm 3 teaches every hunted, betrayed believer to bring real fear honestly to God, to rest in Him as a shield even under threat, and to trust that salvation belongs to the LORD, a confession fulfilled completely when Jesus, betrayed and surrounded by enemies, rose to become salvation itself for His people.

context.literary:
The psalm rests on a chain of contrasts, and the small word "But" at the start of verse 3 is the hinge of the whole. Before it, everything is multiplication: foes have increased, many rise up, many say. After it, everything is singular and personal: You, O LORD, a shield, my glory, the One who lifts my head. The count of the enemies is never disputed. What changes is the address. In verses 1 and 2 David speaks about God's absence to the LORD; in verse 3 he speaks to Him about His presence.

The word "many" is a thread. David counts three times in the first two verses, how many are my foes, how many rise, many say, and then in verse 6 the total is "myriads," ten thousands. The number keeps climbing, and the psalm's structure answers it with a series of single verbs of trust: I cry, He answers, I lie down, I sleep, I wake, I will not fear. Against the crowd, one relationship.

There is also a frame around salvation. The taunt in verse 2 is that there is no salvation for him in God. The psalm ends in verse 8 with the confession that salvation belongs to the LORD. The word yeshuah, help or deliverance, is the opening insult and the closing creed, and the poem is the journey from one to the other. The three selahs mark it as a piece meant to be sung in stages, with a pause after the enemy's speech, a pause after the cry that is heard, and a pause after the final blessing.

The psalm is also arranged around the body. There is a head lifted, a voice raised, a sleeping and waking, and a jaw and teeth struck. The whole person is involved in trust, and the last prayer is for the LORD to deal with the enemy's mouth, the very organ that spoke the taunt.
context.historical:
The superscription gives the psalm a setting, David's flight from his son Absalom, told in 2 Samuel 15 to 18. It was the worst crisis of David's reign, and it came from inside his house. Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel, and the conspiracy gained strength as his following kept increasing, 2 Samuel 15:12. That matches the count of the psalm, where the enemies keep growing. Even David's trusted counsellor Ahithophel went over to Absalom, and David prayed that the LORD would turn his counsel into foolishness, 2 Samuel 15:31.

The king left Jerusalem on foot, crossing the Kidron Valley and climbing the Mount of Olives, weeping, barefoot and with his head covered, 2 Samuel 15:23, 30. On the road Shimei of Saul's family threw stones and cursed him as a man of bloodshed, and told him that the LORD had delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom, 2 Samuel 16:5-8. That is the real-life form of "Many say of me, God will not deliver him." David's answer was not to strike back but to say that perhaps the LORD would see his affliction and repay him with good for the cursing, 2 Samuel 16:12.

The psalm also has a background of guilt. Nathan had told David that the sword would never leave his house, and that adversity would rise from within it, 2 Samuel 12:10-11. The taunters were not entirely wrong that David had given cause. He does not claim to deserve deliverance; he relies on the LORD who is a shield. Another detail is that when the priests brought the ark out, David told them to carry it back to the city, 2 Samuel 15:25, leaving God's presence on Zion, and that is why he can say in verse 4 that the LORD answers him from His holy mountain. Absalom died in the end and David's grief was not triumph, 2 Samuel 18:33.
context.canonical:
Psalm 3 is the first psalm with a title, and the first titled psalm in the Psalter is a lament from a king in a crisis. It joins with Psalm 4, which reads as the evening companion, and both lay down the pattern of the Psalms: fear, cry, answer, rest. The mention of lying down and waking in verse 5 places it as the morning song; Psalm 5:3 opens with the LORD hearing His servant's voice in the morning, so that the early psalms give a day's worth of prayer.

The main words come from earlier in Scripture. The words "Arise, O LORD" in verse 7 recall Moses' prayer when the ark set out, "Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered," Numbers 10:35. David is praying that the ark's prayer be true for him. The image of God as a shield goes back to the promise to Abram, "I am your shield," and forward to prayers such as Psalm 7 and Psalm 18. The blessing at the end recalls the priestly blessing that closes with peace, Numbers 6:24-26.

The psalm's last confession, that salvation belongs to the LORD, is taken up by Jonah from inside the fish, Jonah 2:9, and by the multitude in Revelation, who cry that salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne and to the Lamb, Revelation 7:10. The taunt of verse 2 returns at the cross, where the mockers say, "He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him," Matthew 27:43. And Jesus went out across the Kidron Valley to a garden the night He was betrayed, John 18:1, walking the road David walked, with a traitor among his own.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm was kept in Israel's songbook so that later sufferers could pray with David. The title is not a footnote; it tells the singer that the man praying was a king, in the very hour when his own son had taken the kingdom. If a king could be reduced to that, no one in the congregation could think that trust in God guarantees comfortable circumstances. The setting teaches that faith is not the absence of danger but the ability to lie down within it.

The author also wanted to show what a prayer of confidence sounds like when it is honest. David does not deny the number of his enemies or pretend the taunt is not painful. He repeats the words of the taunters, and then he answers with what he knows about God. That is a method a hearer can copy: name the threat, name the LORD, and speak the second louder than the first.

The closing verse has a further purpose. After a prayer that is entirely personal, David turns outward: may Your blessing be on Your people. A man driven from his throne still prays for the nation that has abandoned him. The psalm teaches the king's heart, which is the heart of a shepherd rather than a survivor.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records what David prayed on a particular night, and the prayer includes a request that God strike the enemies on the jaw and break the teeth of the wicked. That is description of David's cry, and it is not an instruction that believers should ask God to injure their opponents. The New Testament fills out the ethic: Paul says not to avenge ourselves but to leave room for God's wrath, Romans 12:19, and Peter says Jesus, when abused, entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23. The Christian can pray the psalm by handing the matter of justice to God, and by praying for the enemy's good.

David's confidence is also description. He slept, and the psalm reports it. The text does not promise that every believer under pressure will sleep well. Some sleepless nights are honest, as Psalm 44 shows when it asks God to wake up. What the psalm does prescribe by example is where a person takes fear: to the LORD, aloud, and with the expectation of an answer.

debates.question: Does the title give the real setting, or was it added later?

views.label: The title is original and historical
views.case: The details of the psalm, the growing crowd, the taunt that God will not save him, the threat to his life and his ability to sleep, fit the story of 2 Samuel 15 to 18 well, and the title preserves a memory of when David wrote. Most traditional interpreters take this view.

views.label: The title is an early editorial note
views.case: Some scholars think the titles were added by the collectors of the Psalter and reflect an early reading of the poems in light of David's life. On this view the psalm's language is general enough to fit any king in danger and the title invites the reader to see it through 2 Samuel.

views.label: The psalm is a general royal lament
views.case: A third approach reads the psalm as a prayer used by kings in wartime and does not tie it to Absalom, treating the title as later use of the prayer.

debates.bearing: The reading does not change the interpretation. Whether the connection is original or an early reading, the Psalter itself asks us to hear this prayer against the flight from Absalom, and that is how the church has prayed it.

debates.question: What is the meaning of 'Selah'?

views.label: A pause for reflection
views.case: The word may mean a pause or a rest in the music, so that the singer holds what has just been said. In this psalm each selah follows a weighty line, the enemy's taunt, the LORD's answer and the closing blessing.

views.label: A musical lift
views.case: Others connect it to a root meaning to lift up, so that it would mark a rise in voice or instruments. That would suit the way the song moves upward from complaint to trust.

views.label: Uncertain liturgical marker
views.case: Because the ancient translators already disagreed, some interpreters conclude that the exact meaning cannot be recovered and that the word simply signals a break.

debates.bearing: All three uses point to the same effect: the singer is meant to stop and let the last sentence sink in before going on.

study.originalLanguages:
The taunt in verse 2 is worth hearing in the Hebrew. The BSB has "God will not deliver him," and the underlying word is yeshuah, salvation, the same noun that ends the psalm. The enemies say there is no salvation for him in God. David ends by saying salvation belongs to the LORD. The two sentences use the same word and reach opposite verdicts, and the psalm is the road between them.

The image of the shield, magen, in verse 3 is a small shield carried by a soldier. Here it is "around me," which makes the picture different: a shield is normally held in front, and David says the LORD surrounds him on all sides, which answers the enemies "on every side" of verse 6. Two more titles follow. "My glory" is kavod, weight or honor, the mark of a king, and David, stripped of his throne, calls the LORD his honor. The One "who lifts my head" is a phrase for restoration. A head bowed in shame or defeat is lifted by someone else; David does not lift it himself.

In verse 4 "cry aloud" is qara, to call out, and the tense sets it as a habit, so the sense is "whenever I cry aloud, He answers." The answer comes "from His holy mountain," har qodsho, Zion, where the ark was.

Verse 5 has the small verbs of sleep: "I lie down," shakavti, "and sleep," vaishana, "I wake," hekitsoti. The verb "sustains," samakh, is the word for propping something up, as one leans on a support. The LORD props up the sleeper so that he wakes. Nothing in the verb suggests David is strong. He is held.

The number in verse 6 is ribevot, ten thousands, a figure too large to count. Against it David sets no number of his own.

In verse 7 the command "Arise, O LORD" is qumah, the ark-prayer of Numbers 10:35. "Save me" is the verb hoshia, from the root of yeshuah, so that the plea uses the same word as the taunt and the confession. "Strike on the jaw" and "break the teeth" are images of a beast rendered harmless. The Hebrew for "jaw" is lechi, and the point is to silence the mouth that said God would not save.

The final blessing, birkatecha, "Your blessing," is offered on the people, and it is the fitting word, since the psalm began by asking who is truly blessed.

typology.type: David fleeing across the Kidron and up the Mount of Olives, weeping, 2 Samuel 15:23, 30
typology.fulfillment: Jesus crossed the same Kidron Valley on the night of His arrest and went to a garden across it, John 18:1, and He prayed on the Mount of Olives, Luke 22:39-44. Like David, He was betrayed by a close companion, and His enemies gathered against Him. The correspondence is of place, betrayal and trust. The escalation is that David fled from a rebellion he had partly earned, while Jesus went to His arrest deliberately and blameless. The type falls short because David prayed for deliverance from death, but Jesus went into death, and was delivered out of it by resurrection.

typology.type: The taunt, 'God will not deliver him,' Psalm 3:2
typology.fulfillment: At the cross the same words are spoken in almost the same shape: 'He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him,' Matthew 27:43. The mockers of David and the mockers of Christ share a single premise, that the suffering of God's chosen one proves God has abandoned him. The correspondence is remarkably close. The fulfilment is the reverse of what the mockers expected, as God delivers His Son by raising Him from the dead, 1 Corinthians 15:20. The type falls short because David was delivered back to his throne to die a mortal king, while Christ is delivered into an immortal reign.

typology.type: Sleep in the face of danger, Psalm 3:5
typology.fulfillment: David's sleep among enemies looks ahead to the trust of the Son, who could say from the cross, 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit,' Luke 23:46, and who in death is called asleep. Because of His resurrection, Scripture calls Him the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20. The correspondence is of trust in the hour of greatest threat. The escalation is that the sleep David took each night becomes, for believers, the pattern of death itself: it is a sleep from which the LORD wakes them. The type falls short because David's waking was ordinary morning, while Christ's is the first wakening of a new creation.

study.christ:
The clearest bridge is the taunt. The people who said God would not deliver David are answered by the people who stood before the cross and said, "He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him," Matthew 27:43. There is a good reason the Gospel writers record the words; they are the very words of the psalm turned on the Son. What the mockers took for a final verdict was, as in David's case, the beginning of a reversal.

Christ is also the one for whom the prayer is more true than it was for David. David's shield was the LORD; the Son's shield was the Father, in whose hands He committed His Spirit, Luke 23:46. David's head was lifted after the rebellion; Christ's head was crowned with thorns and was lifted by God at the resurrection, Acts 2:32-33. David slept and woke, sustained; the Son died and was raised, and became the firstfruits of those who fall asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20. What David sang in fear, Christ lived to the end.

The psalm's last line reaches its widest meaning in the gospel. "Salvation belongs to the LORD" is not only a statement about who has the power; it says where salvation has to come from. In Jesus, the LORD Himself accomplishes it, and the Greek name Jesus is the Hebrew name meaning the LORD saves. The crowd in Revelation take up the psalm's confession when they cry that salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb, Revelation 7:10.

We should take care not to make every line of the psalm a prophecy about Jesus. The strike on the jaw and the breaking of teeth belong to David's cry and are not put in Christ's mouth, who prayed for those who crucified Him, Luke 23:34. The right link is at the level of pattern: a king betrayed by his own, who trusts the LORD, is mocked and is vindicated. The believer prays this psalm in Christ's company, knowing that the vindication has already been shown.
study.god:
God appears in this psalm as a person who can be spoken to at once. Every line after the opening cry is addressed to Him or about His action. He is not remote. Three roles are given Him in a single verse: shield, glory and the One who lifts the head. Each is a different kind of help. A shield keeps harm out, glory restores honor, and lifting the head restores a person from shame. The God of the psalm meets the whole condition of the sufferer: his safety, his standing and his spirit.

He is a God who answers. The verb in verse 4 is in a form that suggests habit, and David has been heard before. The answer comes from His holy mountain, which locates the God of the psalm in the place of His dwelling with His people. It matters that David has sent the ark back. He does not carry God into exile, because God is not a talisman. The LORD hears from His place, and David, in the wilderness, still reaches Him.

God is a sustainer. The word for "sustains" in verse 5 is supporting, not merely watching. Sleep is a vulnerable state, and no sleeper can guard himself. The psalm teaches that God is the one who keeps watch when the person cannot, a truth stated elsewhere in Psalm 127:1-2 and Psalm 121.

He is also the God who saves and blesses. The last verse joins two things that people often separate: salvation, which is rescue from a specific threat, and blessing, which is an ongoing good on the whole people. The God of the psalm gives both.

For worship, this means the psalm gives words to the person who is scared and outnumbered. It is a fitting prayer for morning after a hard night. It also asks a question of the worshipper: will we believe that our security lies in the LORD, and not in the count of our supporters? The psalm's ending, that salvation belongs to the LORD, is a statement that stops us from looking anywhere else.

crossReferences.note: Absalom sends for Ahithophel and the conspiracy gains strength as his following keeps increasing. It is the history behind the swelling of the foes in verse 1: the enemies are not strangers but the people of David's own kingdom.
The king crosses the Kidron Valley with the people weeping loudly. It fixes the psalm's setting on the road out of Jerusalem and links it with Jesus' own crossing of the Kidron in John 18:1.

Shimei curses David and throws stones, saying the LORD has given the kingdom to Absalom. This is the taunt of Psalm 3:2 heard from the roadside, and David's restraint in 16:11-12 shows the trust the psalm speaks about.

David tells Zadok to take the ark of God back to the city, trusting the LORD to bring him back if he finds favor. It explains why David can say in verse 4 that the LORD answers from His holy mountain, even from the wilderness.

Moses said, 'Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered,' whenever the ark set out. Psalm 3:7 puts David's cry in the same words, asking that what was true for the ark in the wilderness be true for the fugitive king.

Unless the LORD protects the city, watchmen stand guard in vain, and He gives sleep to His beloved. It is the theology of Psalm 3:5 stated as a principle: peaceful sleep is a gift of God, not a reward for being safe.

In God alone my soul finds rest; my salvation comes from Him. It gathers into one line the psalm's closing confession that salvation belongs to the LORD, showing the same trust in another crisis of David's life.

From inside the fish Jonah confesses that salvation is from the LORD. It repeats the closing confession of Psalm 3 from a man in a very different trouble, and shows how the psalm's sentence became a common creed of Israel.

The mockers at the cross say that Jesus trusts in God, so let God deliver Him. It is the taunt of Psalm 3:2 come round again, and the Gospel shows that the mockers were wrong in the same way as David's enemies.
Paul tells believers not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath. It shapes how a Christian prays the imprecation of Psalm 3:7, by giving judgment over to God rather than taking it.

The great crowd before the throne cry out that salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne and to the Lamb. It is the last line of Psalm 3, sung by the redeemed, with the Lamb now named beside God.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 3 places an ordinary human fear inside the story of the covenant. Since Genesis 3 human life has been lived under threat, and since Genesis 4 the threat has often come from those closest. David's flight from Absalom is the story of Cain's murder raised to the level of a throne: a brother, a son, a house at war with itself. The Bible does not hide the pain of that. It records the flight, the curses and the tears, and then it provides a song for the singing.

The psalm also carries forward the covenant promise. God had promised David that his house and throne would last forever, 2 Samuel 7:16, and here that promise is under attack from inside. The taunt that there is no salvation for him in God is a taunt against the promise. The psalm keeps faith with the promise by refusing to let the crisis have the last word. The king may lose Jerusalem for a season; he cannot lose the covenant God.

The gospel takes this psalm to its center. The son of David is betrayed, forsaken by His friends, surrounded, mocked with the same words and put to death. He too commits Himself to His Father, and He is raised. The taunt that God will not deliver Him is refuted by the resurrection, and the confession that salvation belongs to the LORD is filled out, since the LORD Himself has come to save.

The story ends with the crowd that no one could number crying that salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb, Revelation 7:10. In the new creation there is no more night of fear, and no enemy to count. The sleep that David took in the wilderness becomes the rest of the people of God, when He wipes away every tear and there is no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4.

sermon.title: Praying Our Fears
sermon.why: Keller works through Psalm 3, showing how David, with real armies pursuing him, learns to pray his fear rather than be paralyzed by it, tracing the four steps out of the pit in verses 3-8.

quiz.q: What is the crisis David describes at the start of Psalm 3?

options.text: Many foes have risen against him, and many say God will not deliver him.
options.note: This is the psalm's opening complaint, both the number of enemies and their taunt about God.

options.text: He is suffering from a physical illness.
options.note: The psalm's crisis is enemies and betrayal, tied to Absalom's rebellion, not illness.

options.text: He has lost his kingdom to a foreign power.
options.note: The crisis is closer to home, a rebellion led by his own son, not a foreign conquest.

options.text: He has no crisis; the psalm is purely a hymn of praise.
options.note: Verses 1-2 explicitly describe a crisis of many foes and a taunt against his faith.

quiz.q: How does David describe the LORD in verse 3?

options.text: A shield around him, his glory, and the One who lifts his head.
options.note: This threefold description pictures protection and restored dignity.

options.text: A distant king who has not yet responded.
options.note: David describes God as intimately present and protective, not distant or unresponsive.

options.text: A silent witness to his suffering.
options.note: The psalm describes active protection and answered prayer, not mere silent observation.

options.text: An angry judge with no mercy.
options.note: Verse 3 is entirely about protection, glory, and lifted dignity, not wrath.

quiz.q: What surprising thing is David able to do in verse 5, despite being surrounded by enemies?

options.text: Lie down and sleep, and wake again, because the LORD sustains him.
options.note: This is the psalm's striking picture of peace under threat, resting in God's sustaining care.

options.text: Organize a counterattack against his enemies.
options.note: The psalm describes rest and trust in God's care, not a military strategy.

options.text: Flee the country entirely.
options.note: While David has fled Jerusalem historically, the verse itself describes sleeping peacefully, not further flight.

options.text: Give up hope entirely.
options.note: The verse is the opposite of despair; it is a picture of confident rest.

quiz.q: What does David confess in the closing verse of the psalm?

options.text: Salvation belongs to the LORD, and he prays for the LORD's blessing on His people.
options.note: This is the psalm's climactic confession and closing prayer.

options.text: He will save himself by his own strength.
options.note: The psalm explicitly credits salvation to the LORD, not to David's own strength.

options.text: His enemies will never be defeated.
options.note: The psalm's tone is confident hope in God's deliverance, not resignation to defeat.

options.text: The psalm ends without any resolution.
options.note: Verse 8 gives a clear, confident closing confession and blessing.

quiz.q: How does this psalm anticipate Christ?

options.text: David, betrayed by his own son and mocked that God would not save him, foreshadows Jesus, betrayed by Judas and mocked with nearly the same taunt at the cross.
options.note: Matthew 27:43 echoes almost the exact accusation David faced here.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ's life or the New Testament at all.
options.note: Actually the taunt in Matthew 27:43 draws directly on this kind of mockery.

options.text: It only describes generic suffering with no specific New Testament echo.
options.note: The connection is specific: the same accusation, that God will not deliver the sufferer, appears at the cross.

options.text: It predicts the exact date of Christ's crucifixion.
options.note: The psalm draws a thematic and verbal connection, not a chronological prediction.

questions: David brings his real fear, many foes, and a real taunt about his faith, honestly to God rather than hiding it. What fear or doubt are you tempted to hide from God rather than bring to Him in prayer?

David can sleep peacefully even while surrounded by enemies, because the LORD sustains him. What is currently keeping you awake with worry, and what would it look like to entrust that specific fear to God tonight?

David asks God, not himself, to deal with his enemies, appealing to God's justice rather than taking revenge into his own hands. Where do you need to release a desire for personal vengeance and instead trust God's justice?

The psalm closes with salvation belonging to the LORD alone, not to David's own effort or cleverness. Where are you tempted to trust your own strategies for rescue rather than resting in what God alone can do?

Jesus faced betrayal and the same mocking taunt David did, yet trusted the Father completely, even to death. How does knowing that Christ walked this exact path of betrayal and mockery change how you carry your own experiences of betrayal?

translationNotes.note: Selah appears here for the first time in the Psalter; its precise meaning is debated, but it likely functioned as a musical or liturgical pause, inviting reflection at a turning point in the psalm.
The One who lifts my head can describe restoring someone from shame or defeat to honor and confidence, a vivid picture of God reversing the humiliation David's enemies intended for him.

Strike all my enemies on the jaw, break the teeth of the wicked uses animal imagery, picturing enemies as beasts rendered harmless by broken teeth, an appeal for God's justice rather than a description of personal cruelty.
